title: Layouts and Partial Views
description: Reduce duplication and maintain consistent site structure using shared layout pages and partial views.

blocks.text: Every web application has shared elements: a navigation bar, a footer, stylesheets, and scripts. Without layouts, you would copy and paste that markup into every page. Layouts and partial views eliminate that duplication by providing reusable containers.

A layout is the master page that wraps around every view. It defines the HTML skeleton. A partial view is a snippet of reusable markup that you can inject into any layout, view, or page. Together they form the backbone of a maintainable Razor UI.

blocks.title: DRY Principle in Views
blocks.text: DRY means Do Not Repeat Yourself. If you find yourself copying the same nav or footer markup into multiple pages, that is a signal to use a layout or partial view.

A layout page is a Razor file, usually named _Layout.cshtml, that lives in the Shared folder. It contains the shared HTML structure and two special methods: RenderBody and RenderSection. The framework automatically wraps every view inside the layout unless the view chooses otherwise.

blocks.title: A Typical Layout File
blocks.content: The layout defines the HTML skeleton and places for page-specific content.
blocks.code:
Home Products Contact
@RenderBody()

2024 My App. All rights reserved.

@await RenderSectionAsync("Scripts", required: false)

blocks.text: RenderBody is the placeholder where the individual view's content appears. RenderSectionAsync defines optional or required sections that a view can fill. In this layout, the Scripts section is optional, so views that do not need extra JavaScript can omit it.
Setting a Layout from a View

By default, Razor Pages and MVC views use the layout specified in _ViewStart.cshtml. You can also set Layout explicitly inside a view. Setting Layout to null renders the view without any wrapper, which is useful for full-page layouts or API responses.

blocks.title: Overriding the Layout
blocks.content: A view can opt out of the default layout.

blocks.text: A partial view is a Razor file that renders a fragment of a page. It does not have a layout of its own, and it does not define sections. Partial views are perfect for repeated UI elements like product cards, comment threads, or navigation menus.

You can render a partial view in three ways: Html.PartialAsync, Html.RenderPartialAsync, or the partial tag helper. Html.PartialAsync returns an IHtmlContent that you can place inside a view. The partial tag helper is the most modern and readable approach.

blocks.title: Rendering a Partial View
blocks.content: Use the partial tag helper to render a product card.
blocks.code:
@await Html.PartialAsync("_ProductCard", Model.Products[0]) @model Product

@Model.Name

@Model.Price.ToString("C")

View Details

blocks.text: When you use the name="_ProductCard" syntax, Razor searches for the partial in several locations: the same folder as the current view, the Shared folder, and any view location formats you have configured. Naming partials with an underscore prefix is a strong convention that makes them easy to identify.

_ViewStart.cshtml runs before every view in the same folder and subfolders. It is the standard place to set the default layout. _ViewImports.cshtml imports namespaces and injects services so you do not have to repeat them in every view.

blocks.title: ViewStart and ViewImports
When to Use Layouts vs Partials
items: Use a layout when you want a shared page structure like header, footer, and scripts.
Use a partial view when you want to reuse a small UI fragment inside multiple pages.
Use a view component when the fragment needs its own logic or database calls.
Use _ViewStart to set the default layout for a folder hierarchy.

terms.definition: A master Razor file that defines the shared HTML structure for a set of views or pages.
A layout method that outputs the content of the current view inside the layout.
A reusable Razor snippet that renders a fragment of HTML, typically without its own layout.
A Razor file that runs before every view in its folder, commonly used to set the default layout.
A Razor file that imports namespaces and configures tag helpers for all views in its folder.

blocks.title: Exercise: Refactor to a Shared Layout
blocks.description: Extract common markup from multiple pages into a shared layout and a partial view.
steps: Create a new layout file _Layout.cshtml in the Shared folder with a nav, main, and footer.
Move the shared header and footer markup from an existing page into the layout.
Create a _ViewStart.cshtml file that sets Layout = "_Layout".
Create a _ProductCard partial view that renders a product summary.
Use the partial tag helper to render three sample products inside an Index page.
Verify that every page now uses the shared layout and that the product card renders consistently.
blocks.expectedOutcome: The app will have one layout file and one partial view used across multiple pages, removing duplicated markup.

items.text: I know the purpose of RenderBody and RenderSection in a layout.
items.hint: RenderBody inserts the view content; RenderSection inserts named view sections.

items.text: I can render a partial view using the partial tag helper.
I understand how _ViewStart affects view rendering.
items.hint: It runs before each view in its folder to set the Layout property.

items.text: I can choose between a layout and a partial view for a given reuse scenario.
items.hint: Layout for full-page structure, partial for reusable fragments.

blocks.title: Summary
points: Layouts provide a shared HTML skeleton for all pages in a section of the app.
RenderBody and RenderSectionAsync are the two extension points in a layout.
Partial views are lightweight reusable fragments without their own layout.
_ViewStart centralizes layout selection for a folder hierarchy.
_ViewImports centralizes namespaces, tag helpers, and injected services.
blocks.takeaway: Layouts and partial views are the foundation of maintainable Razor applications. Using them from the start keeps your markup clean and your future refactors small.
